reviews.body: ## Why Compaction has always reused the user's selected chat model (`compaction_handler.ts`), with no quality measurement of the summaries it produces. Since compaction blocks the turn mid-stream, both summary quality and generation latency directly shape the agent experience on long chats. This PR adds a compaction-quality benchmark, uses its results to pin a dedicated compaction model for Dyad Pro users, and hardens the compaction prompt against the weakest dimension the benchmark surfaced. ## Benchmark & evidence Methodology in `plans/benchmark-compaction.md`. Eight synthetic-but-realistic AI-coding sessions (~200k est / ~282k actual prompt tokens — right at the production compaction threshold) covering feature marathons, debug spirals with disproven hypotheses, mid-plan refactors, approach pivots, multi-layer migrations, error recovery, sparse early constraints, and tool-noise-heavy sessions. Each fixture carries a ground-truth manifest (tiered facts, superseded-decision "traps", downstream continuation probes). Summaries are generated through the production `COMPACTION_SYSTEM_PROMPT` + `formatAsTranscript` surface and scored by structural checks (including a mechanical file-path hallucination check), a gpt-5.4 fact grid, and probes answered from the summary alone. Full grid (8 fixtures × {gpt-5.6-sol, gpt-5.6-luna} × 2 reps, 0 errors): | | gpt-5.6-sol | gpt-5.6-luna | |---|---|---| | Weighted fact retention (artifact-corrected) | 81% | 83% | | Tier-1 retention | 91% | 93% | | Downstream probe score | 78% | 80% | | Superseded-decision-as-current errors | 0 | 0 | | Hallucinated file paths | 0 | 0 | | **Mean generation wall-clock** | **21 s** | **11 s** | Quality is a statistical tie (per-rep spread up to ±8 pts); latency decides. Luna also matches the existing `SUBAGENT_MODEL` pin, keeping Pro's pinned-model surface to one id. ## Decisions & trade-offs - **Pro-only pin**: the pinned model is only reachable through the Dyad Engine gateway, so non-Pro users keep `settings.selectedModel`. Gating uses `isDyadProEnabled`, same as the explore_code sub-agent's precondition. - **Prompt change ships with the pin, unbenchmarked**: both models' weakest shared dimension was standing user preferences stated once early (50–67% probe scores — e.g. "Tailwind only", "no new deps"), so the prompt gains a dedicated *Standing Preferences & Constraints* section and guideline. The benchmark numbers above were measured on the pre-change prompt; the harness makes a prompt A/B a cheap follow-up. - **Generated transcripts stay local**: the ~800KB-per-fixture transcripts are gitignored; the committed specs + `generate.mjs` regenerate them (manifests/probes are deterministic inputs, only the narrative re-rolls). This keeps 6.7MB out of history at the cost of byte-exact run reproducibility. - **Fake-server routing**: the pin moves compaction requests onto the OpenAI responses handler in tests, which lacked the compaction route; it now recognizes summarize requests before `tc=` fixture matching (the summarized transcript can embed `tc=` markers from earlier turns). ## Running the benchmark ``` CMP_RUN=1 npm run eval -- compaction # full grid (~9M input tokens, ~20 min) CMP_SMOKE=1 npm run eval -- compaction # wiring check ``` Fixture validation runs keyless as part of the suite; regeneration is documented in `src/__tests__/evals/fixtures/compaction/AUTHORING.md`.

reviews.body:
Five commits. A measured performance pass over the two hot paths, a fix for a degenerate case found while stress-testing it, and — since the pass surfaced that tie ordering was never pinned — deterministic nearest-K.

Every change was A/B'd against the previous code with interleaved rounds, and every "faster" variant was checked against the old output before being kept: by grid digest for `build()`, by distance profile for `query_nearest`.

Verified on **Godot 4.4.1, 4.6, 4.7-stable, 4.7-rc and 4.8.dev**. 4.4.1 is the README's stated minimum.

## `build()` — ~1.8-2.0x

Three levers, each isolated and measured separately at N=20000:

| lever | gain |
|---|---|
| cell math + bucket insert inlined out of the `_cell_of`/`_insert` helpers | 1.22x |
| redundant write-back store dropped | 1.13x |
| bounding box accumulated in int locals instead of rebuilding a `Vector2i`/`Vector3i` per point | 1.13x |

## `query_nearest` — ~1.7x (k=1) to ~3.3x (k=32)

The old shape collected every candidate, sorted them once per ring to find the k-th, then ran an O(m·k) selection over the whole list. Profiling said the selection dominated, not the ring walk.

Replaced with a bounded top-k maintained while scanning: a candidate that can't beat the current k-th costs a single compare, and the running k-th distance doubles as the ring stop test — so the per-ring sort and the candidate array both disappear. The walk also traverses the Chebyshev shell directly rather than sweeping the `(2r+1)^dim` block and discarding the interior (3D ring 3: 218 cells, not 343).

Scratch buffers are locals passed as parameters, not fields, so a query still never writes to the grid and concurrent queries stay safe.

## A bound for sparse grids

Ring expansion is output-sensitive and degenerates when `cell_size` sits far below the typical gap between points — reaching the first occupied cell costs O(ring²) probes in 2D, O(ring³) in 3D, all empty. Before this PR, 200 2D queries at `cell_size=0.5` over a 1000-unit spread holding 40 points took **25.6 seconds**; the 3D case didn't finish in a minute.

Reaching ring R probes `(2R+1)^dim` cells, so a one-sweep probe budget collapses to a ring limit computed once. Past it, the query sweeps the occupied cells instead. The top-k is cleared first — that is what keeps the fallback exact, since the sweep revisits cells earlier rings already covered.

Same input now runs in **9 ms**, answer still checked against brute force. Dense path unaffected: 0.99-1.01x.

That limit is integer arithmetic. It previously went through `pow(x, 1.0/3.0)` in 3D, and `pow` carries no correct-rounding guarantee — a one-ulp difference across platforms flips the truncation and changes which path a query takes. (The 2D form used `sqrt`, which IEEE-754 *does* require to be correctly rounded, so that one was already portable — but having both dimensions in integers means neither needs the argument.) It is also cached against the occupied-cell count, so a query pays one int compare rather than a root.

## Deterministic nearest-K

`query_nearest` always returned *a* correct k-nearest set, but which of several **exactly equidistant** points you got was never pinned — ties broke by arrival, and arrival follows insertion history. Same points, two fill orders:

```
build() order    -> [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
reverse add()    -> [11, 10, 9, 8, 7]
```

Identical distances, disjoint identities. Both correct, but the answer wobbles for reasons the caller can't see.

Ties now order by index, so the result is a pure function of the point set and the query — independent of insertion order, removals, and which internal path ran. It landed as opt-in subclasses first (`955dc12`) because the obvious predicate cost 14-18%; reordering it so the common "strictly farther" rejection costs one compare, and only exact ties consult the index, brought that to **0-10%** (1.00x at k=1, 0.90x at k=32). At that price opting in was the wrong shape, so `b82271b` folds it into the base classes and deletes the subclasses.

Deliberately documented as narrowly as I can manage — `query_radius` order still follows bucket order and must be sorted before hashing, the caller's positions must already be bit-identical, and single- vs double-precision engine builds diverge regardless since `Vector2`/`Vector3` are `real_t`.

## What was tried and rejected

`query_radius` is deliberately untouched. Four rewrites were measured and all lost:

| variant | result |
|---|---|
| single-lookup `get(key, default)` | 0.98x |
| hoist `_cells` to a local | 1.00x |
| hand-expanded `dx/dy` instead of `distance_squared_to` | 0.65x |
| whole-cell accept via a corner test | 0.86x |

A reciprocal multiply in `_cell_of` measured exactly 1.00x and would shift boundary cells, so it went too. An attempt to share the bucket loop between the ring walk and the sparse fallback via a `_scan_bucket` helper cost 1.15x on the dense path and was reverted.

## A corrected comment

`_insert` claimed dict-stored packed arrays are copy-on-write and that "the returned array is not a live handle into the Dict". That is wrong — `Variant` holds packed arrays behind a shared refcounted `PackedArrayRefBase *`, so a bucket reached through the Dictionary **is** the stored one. Confirmed empirically on all five engine builds and in `core/variant/variant.h`. The write-backs were dead weight.

## Tests: 296 -> 1010 checks

New coverage targets the paths that had none:

- **sparse clouds** forcing deep ring expansion, where a gap in the shell walk would surface as a silently wrong neighbour set
- **degenerate `cell_size`** — exact against brute force *and* bounded in wall-clock, so a regression fails instead of hangs
- **tie determinism**: insertion-order independence, mid-bucket churn independence, ties resolving to the lowest indices specifically, and cross-cell ties at a `cell_size` small enough to force the sweep fallback
- **`build()` vs a run of `add()`** producing the same grid
- **a direct assertion of the packed-array aliasing** the removed write-backs depend on, so a future engine change fails by name rather than as a lost-index bug inside `remove()`

Shell coverage was also verified exhaustively for rings 0-7 in both dimensions: every cell at Chebyshev distance == ring visited exactly once, no gaps, no duplicates.

## Note for the reviewer

README benchmark numbers were re-captured on a machine under variable load. The ratios are the durable part, not the absolute microseconds.

reviews.body:
**Independent of every other open PR.** Branches from `main`, no behaviour change.

This is #3 reduced to the part @rob-p accepted: the test and build scaffolding, without the packed-key work that PR also carried.

## The crate had no test covering the LCP array

That is the riskiest gap in this codebase. The public entry points discard the LCP array, but the *next* merge level **consumes** it in the three-case decision, so a single wrong entry silently reorders suffixes one level up and the suffix array comes out subtly wrong — permutation intact, order not.

Four tests, checking `lcp[0] == 0` and `lcp[i] == lcp(text[sa[i-1]..], text[sa[i]..])` against a naive oracle over fixtures, random texts across four alphabet sizes, long runs and periodic text, and finite `max_context`.

62 tests before, 66 after.

## The release profile was not what the benchmarks claimed

`bench/README.md` stated the published numbers were taken with `lto = "fat"` and `codegen-units = 1`, supplied by a parent workspace. That workspace is not in this repository. From the commit that made the crate standalone until now, every build made here used `lto = false, codegen-units = 16`, so numbers taken in that window are not comparable with numbers taken since. The profile is pinned here and the stale claim corrected.

In a library crate `[profile.release]` applies only when the crate is the workspace root, so this affects the repo's own tests, examples and benches and is invisible to downstream consumers.

## CI

The repository had no Rust CI, only a docs deploy, while carrying 62 tests with nothing running them.

Runs on `ubuntu-latest` and `macos-latest`, since the LCP kernel and the pooled bucket path are what diverge per platform (x86_64/AVX2 against aarch64/NEON). Tests run in **debug as well as release** — that is not ceremony: debug is what exercises the `debug_assert`s guarding the buffer-length invariants, and on a later branch it caught a `u64` shift-by-64 that release masks to zero and silently gets right. Plus fmt, Clippy with warnings denied, an MSRV check against the declared 1.89, and rustdoc with broken links denied.

The workflow triggers on every branch rather than only `main`. A pull request opened from a fork by a first-time contributor does not run workflows until a maintainer approves them, which is why the API showed no check runs at the tips reviewed in #7; building on push lets the fork produce evidence that can be linked.

## Also

Fixes a pre-existing broken intra-doc link in `build_ext_mem_for_filter`, which pointed at the private `FilteredSource` and would fail the new rustdoc job.

## Review notes from #7, addressed

You asked to correct the stale statement that ruSTAR has not migrated to `SegmentedText` and to clarify that the verifier is for complete plain SAs — both of those live in the packed-key part of #3 and are not in this PR. `verify_sa` is not here either; it belongs with the work that needed it.

## The benchmark described a pipeline that no longer exists

Its numbers were produced by whatever was checked out on 2026-07-10 — before phrase-safe conversion, the corrected script markers, the adaptive buffer and echo removal. Every pipeline fix since then widened the gap between the report and the product.

`pnpm bench -- --repipe` replays the recorded generations through the current assembler **without asking the models for anything**. The checkpoint already kept what the model emitted (`raw`) separate from what the pipeline made of it (`piped`), so this measures the pipeline against identical model output — its effect isolated from sampling noise.

It also **drops the judge scores it invalidates**: the judge grades `engineered` cells on the piped text, so without that a single report would carry scores from two different pipelines.

Re-piped: **17 of 216** generations changed, 6 judge scores re-run.

## What changed in the numbers

Artifacts after the pipeline are now **0% in every model × prompt cell**:

| | before (old pipeline) | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| deepseek-r1 naive, Simplified | 18.5% → 7.4% | 14.8% → **0.0%** |
| qwen3 engineered, Simplified | 11.1% → 7.4% | 3.7% → **0.0%** |
| llama3.1 naive, preamble | 7.4% → 0.0% | 7.4% → 0.0% |

The raw column moved too, because the corrected `SC_MARKERS` no longer counts 系 and 游 as Simplified.

And the pipeline now **adds** chrF on six of eight cells rather than costing it:

| cell | Δ chrF before | Δ chrF after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| llama3.1 naive | −0.3 | **+1.0** |
| deepseek-r1 naive | +2.4 | **+3.3** |
| llama3.1 engineered | −0.5 | −0.1 |

The "reliability layer costs 0.3–0.5 chrF" claim in the README and `docs/BENCHMARK.md` was true of an assembler that flushed mid-artifact and a converter that broke phrases at chunk boundaries. Both are fixed, so the claim is **retired rather than quietly dropped** — the docs now state what replaced it and why.

## Live check first

Before touching the recorded data, eight realistic selections were run through `translateStream` itself against a real qwen3:

- Taiwan vocabulary correct throughout — 網路埠, 資料庫, 記憶體, 預設, 視訊
- a multi-line selection keeps its line breaks (the 2.2.7 flush-point fix, confirmed live)
- no preamble, no echo, no empty output
- an unreachable server still surfaces as the `TypeError` the broker rewrites into the actionable message

211 tests · `tsc --noEmit` clean · `eslint .` clean · `wxt build` clean.

reviews.title: feat(eval): re-score the benchmark through the current pipeline (v2.2.10)

reviews.body:
## What

Publishes the live benchmark results (held local until the numbers were final) and adds the
corpus-poisoning / injection ASR harness that produced the security numbers.

## Harness

- **`engine bench poison-fixture`** — doc-grounded Boardwalk poison fixture, env-tunable
  (`ORCA_POISON_TIER` / `_COPIES` / `_INCLUDE_TRUTH`) for a PoisonedRAG-style sweep into an
  eval-only tenant/kb.
- **`poison-rag.eval.ts`** — measures fact-poison and injection ASR through the real serving
  path (datamark `buildContextBlock` + tier-1 reasoning-off generation, mirroring prod), with
  polarity-exclusive answer markers and a `POISON_DUMP` mode that emits a RAGAS trajectory.
- **evals** — reference-free context-precision added to the RAGAS rails.
- **`bench ingest`** — TCP keepalives + transport-error retry so a 57k-doc corpus survives the
  gateway dropping idle connections.
- **`embed.ts`** — pins the query vector to the column width (`outputDimensionality`) so a
  3072-dim model can be A/B'd without a schema change; inert for Voyage (returns 1024 natively).
- **ledger** — `run_file` stored repo-relative so operator absolute paths don't leak.

## Results (now committed)

- **`RESULTS.md`** — BEIR with voyage-4-large primary (lite annotated) + the gemini A/B.
  voyage-4-large wins first-stage on **both** SciFact (0.718→0.802) and FiQA (0.461→0.565);
  gemini tops near-saturated SciFact but trails on FiQA (0.507 < 0.565) — a saturation artifact,
  and only at the 1024 dims the schema allows.
- **`BENCHMARK-STRATEGY-2026.md`** — the honest publish verdicts:
  - **Injection poisoning held at ASR 0** by the datamark even when 8/8 retrieved slots are the
    untrusted injection ("send 1 ETH to 0x…dEaD"), vs **relayed** when the same content is
    ingested as trusted.
  - **Fact poisoning** is bounded by trust-tier *preference* when the truth is present (ASR ~0
    even at 7/8 flooding) but **not** defended by the spotlight when truth is absent (ASR ~1.0,
    defended ≈ undefended) — stated as the honest boundary.
  - tier-1 **reasoning-off** cost/latency win; BEIR as table-stakes context.
- **`results/{ledger.jsonl, TABLE.md, external-baselines-2026.json}`** — the A/B records, the
  rendered table, and the verified external baselines.

## Verification

- typecheck (8/8), `pnpm -r test` (core 122 / tenant 60 / db 38 / widget 16), engine pytest
  (237 passed / 10 skipped).
- All ASR numbers are answer-verified (the printed answers are ground truth); the marker tally
  was re-run after a polarity-exclusivity pass so the committed harness reproduces them.
- Adversarial multi-lens review of the diff: 7 findings, all fixed (polarity-exclusive markers
  on refund / anti_sniper / redirect / bmx_supply / cliff / fees_fixed; context-precision comment
  corrected to its answer-relative meaning; ledger path relativization). The `embed.ts` Voyage
  no-op was verified against the installed gateway.

## Known follow-up

The RAGAS `Faithfulness` scalar does not complete under the gemini judge (PR #49 swapped it from
Haiku); the metric times out through the gateway. Answer-relevancy + context-precision are
reported; faithfulness-under-misleading-context is measured directly by the C1 probe (5/5) and
the truth-present poison ASR (~0).

reviews.title: Publish live benchmark results + poison/injection ASR harness

reviews.body:
## Description

The published benchmark numbers were stitched together from **two different clusters**. The Production Setup diagram and the changelog carried `93.5 / 148.9 req/s` (from Experiment 1, `e2-standard-4` × 14), while the Benchmark page carried `185.3 / 409.5` for **the same `4 app · 40 w` and `8 app · 80 w` rows** (from a later `n2-standard-16` × 10 run). Same ratio, same flow, different hardware — the two disagreed by 2–3×, and the later scaling run was never recorded in `EXPERIMENTS.md`.

I re-measured all four tiers on one rig, with images built from `main` (`805cc53cf7`, v0.86.3), and torn down afterwards.

### Measured

`n2-standard-16` × 10, `europe-west1-b`, warm, 1:10, 160,000 requests total — **all 200**.

| Apps · Workers | Warm req/s | per worker | Postgres CPU |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 · 40 | 213.0 | 5.3 | 529m / 3000m |
| 8 · 80 | 484.4 | **6.1** | 1096m / 3000m |
| 12 · 120 | 641.0 | 5.3 | 1689m / 3000m |
| 16 · 160 | 777.0 | 4.9 | **2738m / 3000m** |

### Two claims were wrong — rewritten, not renumbered

- **"~4.5 req/s per worker, held flat from 40 to 160 workers — throughput scales linearly."** The per-worker rate peaks at 80 workers and then falls ~20%. This was already contradicted by the page's own table (5.1 → 4.3); the rerun just makes it obvious.
- **"Postgres never crosses ~0.65 of a core […] flat as the fleet quadruples […] no tier approaches saturation."** Postgres climbs 529m → 2738m, ending at **91% of its 3-core reservation**, and is what bends the curve. Its cost is ~2.5 millicores per req/s, so it scales with *throughput* and no setting stops it. Workers meanwhile idle at ≤0.1 of their 0.5-core cap.

Production Setup now warns to size the database against peak throughput, and notes that a **managed** 2 vCPU Postgres with real durability will hit its ceiling *earlier* than this deliberately over-provisioned rig did.

### Load is now generated in-cluster

Driving 120+ concurrent sync webhooks from a workstation exhausts its ephemeral port range (macOS ~16k; `hey` dies with `can't assign requested address`) and **fabricates a cliff at exactly the 120-worker tier** — 252 req/s, *below* the 80-worker row — while the cluster sits healthy. External and in-cluster runs agree at 40 workers (214.7 vs 213.0) and diverge above 80.

This is the likely origin of the "120 cliff" previously credited to Postgres `max_connections=100`: it reproduces with `max_connections=2000`. I've corrected that explanation rather than restating it.

### Rig fixes (each silently corrupted a re-run)

- `run-gke.sh` minted a fresh random `AP_JWT_SECRET` per run but restarted **only** the worker. `envFrom` is read once at container start, so app pods kept the old secret, every worker socket handshake failed with `Authentication error`, and **workers never recover from it** — pods `Running`, fleet "ready", nothing consuming jobs, flow publish dying 300 s later. Now: restart app → await rollout → restart workers.
- The per-run breakdown parsed JSON, but the worker ignores `AP_LOG_PRETTY` and always uses the pretty renderer, so it reported "no timing samples". (Which means the old latency table cannot have come from this parser.)
- The breakdown scraped `--since=20m`, folding cold boot and the warmup pass into the "warm" averages. Now scoped to the measured pass.
- Manifest pointed at bucket `ap-bench-usc-b3803` / `us-central1` — **deleted** — while its own comments and the docs said `europe-west1`; `ZONE` defaulted to `us-central1-a` and `APP_CPU` to `1500m` against a documented 1 vCPU.
- `production-setup.mdx` listed the app as 1 vCPU / **2 GB** while its own sizing example and the benchmark both say 1 GB.
- The CLI section claimed its 4-worker sample run came "from the results table", which has no 4-worker row.

Full method, results and traps are recorded in `benchmark/EXPERIMENTS.md` as **Experiment 3** — this experiment previously had no entry at all.

## How was this tested?

Docs-and-tooling only; no product code changed, so no edition paths apply.

- Ran the full 4-tier sweep end to end on a real GKE cluster (created and torn down for this PR); every number in the diff comes from that run's logs.
- Tier 1 measured three times (220.8 / 217.7 / 214.7 req/s externally, 213.0 in-cluster) — reproducible to ±1.5%.
- `bash -n benchmark/run-gke.sh`; `benchmark/k8s-sandbox.yaml` parses (8 docs) with the worker env intact.
- `worker-scaling.png` re-rendered from its committed HTML source via headless Chrome and visually checked.
- Cluster, load balancer, disks and the run's HMAC key all confirmed deleted — nothing left billing.

Fixes # (issue)

### Breaking change?  (required — CI fails if this is left unedited)

- [x] no — reviewed, not breaking
- [ ] yes — technical (removed/renamed API field or endpoint, dropped column, new required field, removed/required env var)
- [ ] yes — functional (default/limit/behaviour change, new self-hosted setup step)

### Security impact?  (required — CI fails if this is left unedited)

- [x] no — reviewed, no security impact
- [ ] yes — security-sensitive (call out the risk and mitigation in the description above)

## Summary

Applies the advisor's 8 recommended edits to `docs/findings/model-updates-2026-05.md` (session 68 model survey), plus cascading updates to memory and tracking files.

**Core theme:** The advisor identified that benchmark numbers and Ollama tag claims were sourced from secondary blogs, not primary sources. The risk is treating unverified blog claims as engineering commitments (persona migrations, DECISIONS.md edits, models.yaml deprecations). These changes invert the order: verify locally first, commit to swaps second.

## Changes in `docs/findings/model-updates-2026-05.md`

1. **Methodology footnote at top** — warns that many existence/benchmark claims come from secondary sources; points to `ollama.com/library/<tag>` for verification
2. **TL;DR re-framed** — "P0 — Swap" → "P0 — Pull + Benchmark" and "P0 — Pull + Probe"; swap/probe explicitly conditional on local validation
3. **Verification Status column** — added to TL;DR with 5-value legend (`verified-tag`, `tag-unverified`, `bench-unverified`, `bench-medium`, `inferred-from-blog`)
4. **Qwen3.7 Max qualified** — single-source origin flagged; unusual naming convention noted; verify from official Qwen blog before acting
5. **Benchmark numbers footnoted** — ~88%/~62% (qwen3.6-coder) and ~85%/~55% (qwen2.5-coder) marked as secondary-source claims with ¹ notation; footnote notes the official Qwen2.5-Coder report had ~90% — if baseline is wrong, the delta is artificially narrowed
6. **Embedding probe = hard gate** — LTG Phase 2 impact table updated: bge-m3 (0.6GB) → qwen3-embedding:8b (~5GB) changes VRAM math significantly; old WARN verdict doesn't apply; new probe required before embed.py
7. **Llama 4 Scout 10M context qualified** — effective useful range for RAG ~200K–1M, not 10M; still a step change over current 128K ceiling
8. **Independent benchmark Y/N column** — added to all 3 frontier-distilled tables; ✅ Yes for DeepSeek-R1 (official paper); ❌ No for all Jackrong and TeichAI community models
9. **Changes-made response section** — added at doc bottom with table mapping each advisor point to the change applied

## Cascading Updates

|---|---|
| `.memories/QUICK.md` | "supersedes (~88%)" → "candidate to supersede (secondary source; gated on M-P0a)"; probe marked hard gate |
| `.memories/KNOWLEDGE.md` | Benchmark numbers qualified; embedding probe hard gate noted |
| `.claude/tasks.md` | M-P0a: benchmark-first framing; M-P0b: hard gate + "Do not start embed.py until probe passes"; M-update: deprecation gated on confirmed benchmark |

| `.claude/session-log.md` | Session 69 entry added |
| `.claude/index.md` | Model survey entry updated to mention advisor review section |

## Test plan

- [ ] Verify `docs/findings/model-updates-2026-05.md` renders correctly — tables with new columns, footnotes, blockquotes
- [ ] Confirm TL;DR P0 rows read "Pull + Benchmark" and "Pull + Probe" (not "Swap")

Closes nidus-132.

Eleven documentation coverage gaps left over from the 2026-08 audit (PR #129 landed the
surgical correctness fixes and the em dash sweep). Every claim was re-derived from `src/`,
`sdks/`, and `charts/` rather than trusted, because nothing in CI diffs docs prose against
the route table, the CLI flag surface, the SDK method surface, or the env vars: `docs.yml`
only builds Astro.

## What landed

- **`reference/cli.md`** (new page, + sidebar entry): all 23 subcommands with every flag,
  each flag's `NIDUS_*` binding, and the feature gating that matters (a `--features cli`
  build has no `--embed-*`/`--summarize-*`/`mcp`/`remember`/`recall`; the binstall binary,
  built `--features serve`, has them all).
- **`reference/http-api.md`**: `POST /remember` and `/recall` (`ttl_seconds`,
  `dedupe_threshold`, the redirected id on a dedupe match) plus the `/mcp` mount.
- **`sdks/javascript.md`**: rewritten against the real client (remember/recall,
  `batchSearch` + fuse, `aggregate`, the full options surface, `v.float`/`v.datetime`).
- **`sdks/python.md`** + **`sdks/go.md`**: the Go `Remember` example now compiles against
  `(RememberResult, error)`; `batch_search`/`aggregate` and remember's ttl/dedupe added.
- **`reference/api.md`**: the missing public types, including the backend traits that
  `storage-backends.md` and `memory-stores.md` already promised were documented here.
- **`guides/kubernetes.md`**: the three replica topologies and the Ingress/TLS example
  `http-server.md` pointed at.
- **`guides/http-server.md`**: the `NIDUS_*` table completed from 18 to all 48, grouped by
  family, plus a text-native-ingest section with its failure modes.
- **`index.mdx`**: the server, MCP, and SDKs are now reachable from the front door.
- **`guides/remember-and-recall.md`**: a memory-parity matrix across Rust/HTTP/MCP/CLI.
- **`guides/how-it-works.md`**: the index-cache lifecycle.
- **`reference/performance.md`**: `persist_index` documented as manual, plus measured
  FTS/hybrid/`rank_by` numbers from three new benchmarks.

## Three corrections to the epic body

The ticket was stale against the tree, so the pages follow source, not the ticket:

| nidus-132 said | Tree says |
|---|---|
| 18 CLI subcommands | 23 |
| ~45 `NIDUS_*` vars | 46 clap-declared plus 2 read in `src/diag.rs` |
| `/ready`, `/cluster`, `/refresh`, `/metrics` untyped in the SDKs | only `/metrics`, deliberately |

## Benchmarks

`bench_text_search`, `bench_hybrid` (sweeping `candidates`) and `bench_rank_by` (a
with/without delta, single-threaded) in `benchmarks/benches/nidus_regression.rs`. The
published numbers were measured on an idle machine, not taken from the agent run that
produced the code. Reproduce with a single regex filter, since criterion's harness takes
only one positional argument:

```
cargo bench -p nidus-bench --bench nidus_regression -- 'text_search|hybrid|rank_by'
```

## No version bump

`laws.mjs` `BEHAVIOURAL` covers `^src/`, `^sdks/`, `^Cargo.toml$`, `^Dockerfile$`,
`^install.sh$`. This change touches only `docs/` and `benchmarks/`. Docs deploy through
`docs.yml` independently of `release.yml`, and benchmarks are never published, so a bump
would cut a release containing no shipped code change. `nidus-check laws` reports 0 errors.

## Verification

`just docs-build` green (24 pages), `nidus-check laws` 0 errors, `cargo fmt --check` and
`clippy -p nidus-bench --all-targets -D warnings` clean, the three new benches run to
completion.

`/nidus review` confirmed three factual-drift defects, all fixed and re-verified against
source before this push: `cli.md` called the `--max-concurrent-requests` default unbounded
when `resolve_concurrency(0)` returns `8x` cores floored at 64; six JS examples passed a
bare `Predicate` where `Filter = Predicate[]` is required, so they would not compile; and
the `recall --min-score` rows said "at or below" when the kernel compares `score < min` and
keeps ties.

Two further defects found during the merge, neither of which any CI job would catch: stale
prose in `remember-and-recall.md` claiming `Summarize` stores the original under
`nidus.source` (it stamps `nidus.summary` and `nidus.text`), contradicting the new parity
matrix on the same page; and a wrong ticket citation crediting the `nidus.source` change to
nidus-131 rather than nidus-133.

Filed separately as **nidus-l8k**: the same "at or below" wording is wrong in `src/` too,
at `src/memory.rs:86` and `src/cli/mod.rs:981`, so `nidus recall --help` currently
contradicts the corrected reference page. Left out of this PR because it touches `src/`,
which would pull a version bump into a docs-only change.

reviews.body:
Adds a runtime benchmark suite, then uses it to make the container substantially faster. The two are in one PR because the second half is only trustworthy given the first — and because building the harness immediately exposed two ways it was lying.

## Results

Measured with `pnpm bench` (added here), before vs. after, on the same machine:

| benchmark | before | after | |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `add` chain of 200 | 2,158 hz | 21,433 hz | **9.9× faster** |
| `add` chain of 100 | 9,062 hz | 47,210 hz | 5.2× |
| `compose` 20 pre-built modules | 13,859 hz | 32,547 hz | 2.4× |
| cached `get()` — 100 deps | 33,389 hz | 88,979 hz | **2.7× faster** |
| cached `get()` — 3 deps | 65,759 hz | 88,612 hz | 1.35× |
| property access | 43,629 hz | 55,076 hz | 1.26× |
| `clone` a 200-dep container | 43,794 hz | 34,561 hz | **0.79× — slower** |

## The main change

`add` rebuilt the entire resolver map on every call (`{ ...this.resolvers, [name]: resolver }`), making a chain O(N²) at runtime for the same reason it is O(N²) to type-check. `merge` did the same once per merged container. Both now write in place.

That is only safe because of an invariant the code did not previously enforce: **`clone()` handed the clone its source's actual map object**, and the two stayed independent only because every write happened to allocate a replacement. `setResolvers` now copies, and three new tests in `clone.test.ts` pin it in both directions — they fail without the copy.

Smaller wins, all measured:

- `get()` no longer reads the resolved-value cache twice. Worth roughly 2× on a large container, where the map is in V8's dictionary mode and each read is a hash lookup.
- The context `Proxy` no longer calls `.toString()` on every dependency a factory destructures. Symbols now pass through as symbols rather than being looked up under their description.
- The copies in `setResolvers` are entry-by-entry loops rather than spreads — measured 2.4× cheaper for a dictionary-mode map, which is what took `clone` from 0.39× back to 0.79×.

### The `clone` regression is deliberate

It is the irreducible cost of the extra map copy that makes in-place `add` safe: 59 µs → 29 µs to clone a 200-dependency container, a rare operation, in exchange for wins on `add` and `get`, which every consumer pays on every use. Flagging it rather than burying it.

## Two harness bugs found while building the benchmarks

Both were making the numbers lie, and the first predates this PR.

**1. Vitest was running every suite twice.** `tsc` compiles the tests alongside the sources, and Vitest 4 dropped `**/dist/**` from its default excludes — so each suite ran once from `src/` and again from whatever the last build emitted into `dist/`. That is why `pnpm test` reported 16 files for 8. It also means a stale `dist/` could pass a suite the sources fail. Fixed with a `vitest.config.ts`.

**2. The cached-resolution benchmarks were measuring V8's optimiser.** Resolving one fixed name in a batch leaves the call loop-invariant, and V8 hoists it clean out of the loop — in the old build but not the new one. That artefact reported the 2.7× `get()` speedup above as a *1.6× regression*, reproducibly, in both directions. The rows now vary the name per iteration.

The corrected direction was confirmed independently of Vitest, in isolated processes against both compiled builds: 25 ns → 6 ns per cached `get()` at 100 dependencies, stable across alternating runs.

## Notes for review

- No public API or type changes; `dist/` output is unchanged in shape.
- Zero runtime dependencies preserved; the benchmark suite is dev-only and excluded from the published package by the existing `files` rule.
- `pnpm build`, `pnpm test`, `pnpm lint` and `pnpm bench:types` all pass; type-instantiation budgets are unmoved.
- Benchmarks are deliberately **not** wired into CI — wall clock does not transfer between machines, which is the same reasoning `docs/type-benchmarks.md` already gives for gating the type budgets on instantiations instead of time.
reviews.title: perf: linear wiring and faster cached resolution, with a benchmark suite to prove it

reviews.body:
WP2b of the 0.3.0 search-pipeline hardening program. References epic #75. Built on top of the in_force/abstain modes (PR #80).

## Findings fixed

**(a) Penalized expansion backfill (main false-positive vector).** Query expansion (synonym #38 + co-occurrence #40) previously folded derived terms into the single FTS5 `MATCH`. FTS5 bm25 has no positional preference, so a doc matching only a synonym received full idf weight and could outrank a doc matching the user's actual term — the "appended = down-weighted" claim in the module docstrings was false. `Index.search` now runs the user's own terms as a PRIMARY `MATCH` and the expansion terms in a SEPARATE penalized backfill pass (`_expansion_backfill`) whose hits can only rank BELOW the worst primary hit. The docstrings in `query_expansion.py` / `cooccurrence.py` are corrected.

**(b) Co-occurrence defaults hardened.** `min_count` 2→3, `min_pmi` 0.0→0.1; added a corpus-size floor (`KB_COOCCURRENCE_MIN_DOCS`, default 50) that auto-disables the table on small corpora where PMI is noise, and a per-doc unique-token cap (`KB_COOCCURRENCE_MAX_DOC_TOKENS`, default 400) bounding the O(n²) pair counting so a multi-thousand-word doc is no longer a build-time memory cliff.

**(c) Gated trigram index.** `fts_trigram` (a full second tokenized copy of the corpus, ~2-3× index-size / build-time tax) is now created and populated ONLY when the trigram fallback is enabled (`KB_TRIGRAM_MODE=on`), not unconditionally. A default deployment pays no trigram cost.

**(d) Rank-class invariant made true.** `SearchHit` gained `rank_class` (`RANK_CLASS_PRIMARY` / `RANK_CLASS_BACKFILL`). The status and hybrid rerankers now sort by `(rank_class, score)`, so a backfill (expansion/trigram) hit can never be reordered above a primary — even when a reranker ADDS status deltas or RE-NORMALISES scores. The previous score-only "strictly worse" floor could be lifted by an active-status boost or the hybrid blend. The trigram module docstring is corrected accordingly.

**(e) Status prior.** Left as the intended quality knob (in_force hard filtering from #80 covers the correctness-critical case). The status reranker is now rank-class-aware and tested; no calibration change was needed to make it sane.

**(f) Dense channel includes intent vocabulary.** The text embedded at build time now includes `applies_when` and `tags` (the curated intent phrases a paraphrase query embeds near), not just title/description/body.

**(g) Vector perf.** The id→vector matrix is loaded from SQLite ONCE per build and cached (keyed by db file (size, mtime), invalidated transparently by the atomic swap). This removes the per-candidate `get_vector` connection the hybrid reranker used to open and the per-query full-table re-read in `dense_candidates`.

**(h) `>limit` bug.** `search()` now truncates to `limit` unconditionally. Previously truncation lived only inside the reranker branch, so with embeddings configured but no reranker set the dense union could return more than `limit` hits.

**(i) Build perf.** `Index.build` runs a single `git log --name-only` pass for every file's last-commit time (one subprocess instead of N) and reads + parses each markdown file exactly once (was three times: two parses plus a separate content read). Per-file `(last_modified, source)` metadata is byte-for-byte identical; the batched pass uses `-z` NUL-delimited output with `core.quotePath=false` so filenames with spaces/unicode round-trip exactly rather than falling back to mtime.

**(j) Malformed frontmatter surfaced.** A doc whose front-matter block is present but is invalid YAML (so its `status`/`supersedes` are silently dropped, quietly disabling staleness protection) is now logged at WARN per doc, counted, and surfaced via `Index.malformed_frontmatter_count` and the `malformed_frontmatter` field in `health()`. A doc with genuinely no front matter is not counted.

## Test evidence

New `tests/test_search_hardening.py` plus updates to `test_trigram.py` / `test_cooccurrence.py`:
- (a) expansion-only hit never outranks a primary (with rank_class assertions).
- (d) status AND hybrid rerankers keep backfill below primaries even with an active-status / perfect-cosine backfill hit.
- (b) corpus floor / threshold behavior; hardened defaults.
- (c) trigram table absent when off, present when on, and off-build strictly smaller than on-build.
- (h) `>limit` regression (embeddings on, no reranker).
- (f) embedded text asserted to include `applies_when` + tags.
- (g) vector matrix loaded ≤1× per query; cache invalidated on rebuild.
- (i) batched git timestamps equal per-file query results; special-char filename resolves via git; non-git KB falls back to mtime.
- (j) malformed-frontmatter counter + health field; no-frontmatter not counted.

Full suite + `ruff` + `mypy` all green. Rebased onto latest `origin/release/0.3.0`; CHANGELOG conflict resolved keeping all entries.

## Peer review (codex)

First pass: **0 Blockers**, 2 Concerns, 2 Nits. All verified points confirmed correct (expansion backfill flow, gated trigram with no code path assuming its existence, `>limit` fix, vector batch fetch removing per-hit connections, no committed benchmark numbers touched). All four items were fixed:
- Concern (git-path exactness): switched to `-z` NUL-delimited + `core.quotePath=false`, no path `.strip()`; added a special-char-filename regression test.
- Concern (hybrid rank-class not directly tested): added a pure hybrid-reranker test (perfect-cosine backfill at weight=1.0 must stay below a weak-cosine primary).
- Nit: corrected the stale `config.py` "trigram always built" comment.
- Nit: strengthened `test_trigram_hits_appended_after_primary` to assert primaries precede backfill via rank_class.

Second pass empirically confirmed the git-parser byte structure matches the implementation. No Blockers at any point.
reviews.title: fix(search): penalized expansion backfill, gated trigram build, dense-channel and build perf fixes

reviews.body:
Builds on the v0 foundation in `main` (working MCP server + accuracy-audited benchmark) with the
differentiator pillar and a way to measure the routing lever.

## What's in this PR
**CCI / Context Packs** (`d12a581`) — the living-docs differentiator. 3 new MCP tools:
- `repo_map` — token-budgeted map of the most-referenced symbols (PageRank proxy over the code graph)
- `get_context` — read the module's `.context/*.md` Context Pack (layered, walks up the tree)
- `update_context` — persist distilled domain logic to `<module>/.context/domain_logic.md`

The agent writes what it learned after a task (synthesis by its own model — no extra key), staged
into the PR so review covers the context too; the next agent reads ~1k tokens instead of the module.
Write→read round-trip verified via `test/client.ts` (7 tools total now).

**GitHub Models provider + footprint doc** (`758d22c`):
- GitHub Models wired into the benchmark (free, OpenAI-compatible, PAT with `models` scope) so the
  model-routing lever (gpt-4o vs gpt-4o-mini) is finally measurable — the gap Gemini's free tier left.
- `docs/infra/footprint-and-deployment.md`: measured RAM/CPU/disk (~31 MB idle, transient per-call
  spikes) and the local-first deployment decision.

## Verification
- `bun run test:client` — server boots, all 7 tools list + return real results; CCI round-trip passes.
- `bun run smoke` (offline) and `bun run src/microbench.ts` (no API) reproduce.

## Honest notes
- Benchmark numbers were corrected after an adversarial 5-lens audit: structural retrieval wins
  (~97%); naive semantic search is NOT a token win vs scoped grep (measured, not assumed).
- Caching + premium-vs-cheap routing need a paid/Anthropic or GitHub Models token to measure live.

### [`v8.4.67`](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/releases/tag/v8.4.67): - Add opt-in weights_only model loading via ULTRALYTICS_SAFE_LOAD (#​24829)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/compare/v8.4.66...v8.4.67)

#### 🌟 Summary

v8.4.67 is a **small but meaningful release** focused on **safer model loading** 🔒, plus an important **TT100K dataset label fix** 🛣️ and a batch of documentation/link cleanups 📚.

#### 📊 Key Changes

- 🔒 **New opt-in safe model loading via `ULTRALYTICS_SAFE_LOAD`** ([@​glenn-jocher](https://redirect.github.com/glenn-jocher), PR [#​24829](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/issues/24829))
  - Ultralytics added a new environment flag, `ULTRALYTICS_SAFE_LOAD=true`, that enables a safer way to load model checkpoints.
  - When enabled, checkpoint loading uses PyTorch’s newer `weights_only=True` behavior and only rebuilds **known Ultralytics and PyTorch model classes** from an automatically generated allow-list.
  - This replaces the older unused `SafeUnpickler` approach.
  - **Important:** this is **off by default**, so existing workflows keep working as before.

- 🛣️ **TT100K dataset class list corrected to the official 221-category set** ([@​glenn-jocher](https://redirect.github.com/glenn-jocher), PR [#​24718](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/issues/24718))
  - The `TT100K.yaml` dataset config had duplicated and incorrect class names.
  - That caused some class IDs to silently lose labels during conversion, even though training still proceeded.
  - The release now aligns TT100K with the official upstream category list, including missing real classes.

- 📘 **Rust inference docs updated to `ultralytics-inference 0.0.21`** ([@​onuralpszr](https://redirect.github.com/onuralpszr), PR [#​24825](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/issues/24825))
  - Documentation examples now point to the latest Rust inference crate version.

- 🔗 **Many documentation links were refreshed and corrected** ([@​glenn-jocher](https://redirect.github.com/glenn-jocher), PR [#​24824](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/issues/24824) and [#​24817](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/issues/24817))
  - Updated links across integrations, datasets, examples, and guides.
  - Includes a fix for the CoreML NMS glossary link and many canonical URL updates.

#### 🎯 Purpose & Impact

- 🔐 **Safer checkpoint loading for security-conscious users**
  - The new opt-in safe loading mode helps reduce risk when loading model files by allowing only recognized model components.
  - This is especially useful for teams working in stricter environments or aligning with newer PyTorch defaults.
  - Because it is **optional**, users with custom or forked architectures are **not disrupted**.

- ♻️ **Better future compatibility with PyTorch**
  - PyTorch 2.6+ is moving toward `weights_only` loading by default.
  - This update helps Ultralytics stay aligned with that direction while preserving backward compatibility today.

- 🚫 **Less chance of silent dataset errors**
  - The TT100K fix is a big quality improvement for anyone training on that traffic-sign dataset.
  - Previously, some categories could effectively receive no labels without an obvious crash.
  - Now, dataset conversion and training should be much more trustworthy 🎯

- 🧰 **Minimal disruption for most users**
  - No major model architecture changes were introduced in this tag.
  - Standard loading behavior remains unchanged unless you explicitly enable safe loading.
  - Most other changes are documentation polish, so the release is low-risk and practical ✅

- 📚 **Clearer onboarding and fewer broken docs**
  - Updated links and version references make tutorials and integration guides easier to follow, especially for newer users.

If you want, I can also provide a **one-paragraph release note version** or a **developer-focused summary** of v8.4.67.

### [`v8.4.66`](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/releases/tag/v8.4.66): - Add `nvidia-ml-py` to pyproject.toml (#​23922)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/compare/v8.4.65...v8.4.66)

#### 🌟 Summary

Ultralytics **v8.4.66** improves built-in **NVIDIA GPU monitoring reliability** 🔋, adds better **semantic segmentation class filtering and metrics** 🧠, and enhances **CoreML semantic exports** on iPhone with full-resolution outputs 📱.

#### 📊 Key Changes

- **Main update: NVIDIA GPU monitoring is now more reliable** 🚀
  - `nvidia-ml-py` was added as a standard dependency by [@​glenn-jocher](https://redirect.github.com/glenn-jocher).
  - GPU stats collection now uses NVIDIA’s NVML library directly instead of trying to install support at runtime.
  - This affects built-in GPU reporting in utilities like auto device selection and system logging.

- **Semantic segmentation got a meaningful feature upgrade** 🎯
  - The `classes` filter now works properly for **semantic segmentation** during:
    - dataset loading
    - prediction
    - validation
    - metric reporting
  - Non-selected classes are cleanly ignored instead of being mixed into results.
  - Added safeguards for unsupported cases like `single_cls=True` in semantic segmentation.

- **Semantic segmentation metrics are more accurate** 📈
  - mIoU now ignores classes that are not actually present in the ground truth.
  - Per-class reporting was improved so summaries better reflect what was really evaluated.

- **CoreML semantic exports now keep full-resolution maps** 📱✨
  - CoreML exports for semantic segmentation now output full-resolution semantic maps instead of lower-resolution stride-8 maps.
  - This means much sharper segmentation overlays on Apple devices like iPhones.

- **Updated iPhone CoreML benchmark docs** 📊
  - Performance numbers were refreshed using optimized profile-mode measurements.
  - Documentation now better reflects real YOLO26 CoreML behavior, especially for semantic models.

- **TensorRT 11 export flow was simplified** ⚙️
  - The separate `half` argument was removed from ONNX precision conversion.
  - TensorRT 11 export now has a cleaner path for FP16 and INT8 generation.
  - INT8 calibration preprocessing was streamlined for cleaner and more maintainable export behavior.

- **Documentation improvements across YOLO26 guides** 📝
  - The **Model Testing** guide was rewritten for clarity and accuracy.
  - The **YOLO26 Training Recipe** guide was improved to better explain how official checkpoints were trained.
  - Small fixes were also made to JupyterLab and SAM 3 docs.

- **CI and packaging cleanup** 🛠️
  - CI dependency installs now retry automatically, reducing flaky failures.
  - Since `nvidia-ml-py` is now a standard dependency, extra manual installs were removed from CI and Docker setup.

#### 🎯 Purpose & Impact

- **More dependable GPU stats for users with NVIDIA hardware** ✅\
  Users should see fewer issues with built-in GPU monitoring, logging, and hardware-aware utilities because the required NVIDIA package is now installed up front instead of handled on the fly.

- **Better usability for semantic segmentation workflows** 🎨\
  If you work with semantic segmentation and only care about certain classes, filtering now behaves much more intuitively during prediction and evaluation.

- **More trustworthy segmentation metrics** 📏\
  Reported semantic segmentation scores are now less misleading, especially on datasets where some classes are absent or filtered out.

- **Sharper CoreML semantic results on iPhone and Apple devices** 🍎\
  Semantic masks should look much cleaner and less blocky, improving visual quality for mobile deployment.

- **Cleaner export experience for TensorRT 11** ⚡\
  Developers exporting models for NVIDIA deployment get a simpler and more maintainable precision conversion workflow.

- **Clearer docs for a broader audience** 📚\
  New and experienced users alike should find YOLO26 testing, training, and deployment guidance easier to follow.

Overall, **v8.4.66** is a practical quality-focused release: it strengthens GPU monitoring, improves semantic segmentation behavior, and brings better mobile export quality without changing the core user workflow.

### [`v8.4.65`](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/releases/tag/v8.4.65): - QNN channel-last + semantic ArgMax performance improvements (#​24790)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/compare/v8.4.64...v8.4.65)

#### 🌟 Summary

v8.4.65 is mainly a **mobile inference performance release** 📱⚡, with the biggest upgrade improving **QNN exports for Snapdragon NPUs** and speeding up **semantic segmentation outputs** by moving costly work inside the model graph.

#### 📊 Key Changes

- 🚀 **Major QNN export performance upgrade** in PR [#​24790](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/issues/24790) by [@​glenn-jocher](https://redirect.github.com/glenn-jocher)
  - QNN exports now use **channel-last (NHWC) input**, which better matches Qualcomm Hexagon NPU hardware and camera-native image layouts.
  - This avoids extra data reordering at inference time, reducing overhead on both the app side and the NPU side.
  - Implemented through new export wrappers like `QNNModel` instead of fragile post-export graph editing.

- 🧠 **Semantic segmentation exports are much faster on-device**
  - For **QNN** and **CoreML** semantic models, export now embeds **ArgMax / class-map generation directly in the graph**.
  - Instead of returning large floating-point logits that apps must decode afterward, exported models can now return a compact **per-pixel class map** directly.
  - New `ClassMapModel` wrapper handles this behavior during export.

- 📱 **Better mobile runtime compatibility**
  - Semantic predict/validation code was updated so Ultralytics can correctly handle both:
    - traditional logits outputs
    - new exported class-map outputs
  - This makes the faster export behavior work more cleanly across deployment and evaluation workflows.

- 📉 **Measured impact highlighted in docs**
  - QNN semantic performance became much more stable, replacing previously erratic decoding times with far more predictable behavior.
  - CoreML semantic exports also saw notable end-to-end speedups from in-graph class-map generation.

- 🛠️ **RKNN export improvements**
  - RKNN export now properly supports **FP16 intermediate ONNX export**.
  - Added **RKNN INT8 export test coverage** to improve reliability.
  - RKNN export docs/tables were updated accordingly.

- 🐳 **Docker build reliability improvements**
  - Dockerfiles now use more cache-conscious install patterns and extra cleanup steps to reduce disk pressure during builds.
  - The Docker workflow was simplified by removing an extra assistant-trigger step.

- 📚 **Docs and export guidance improvements**
  - Expanded and refreshed docs for **CoreML** and **QNN**, including clearer deployment guidance and performance notes.
  - Export docs now better explain **YOLO26 end-to-end detection output formats**.
  - Tracking docs now clarify support for **OBB models** as well.
  - Rust inference docs were updated to `ultralytics-inference` version `0.0.19`.

- ✅ **CI and workflow fixes**
  - Docs redeploys now trigger more reliably when documentation changes land on `main`.
  - CUDA training tests are now explicitly skipped on Jetson devices, making CI behavior cleaner and easier to maintain.

#### 🎯 Purpose & Impact

- ⚡ **Faster mobile inference on Snapdragon devices**\
  Users deploying YOLO on Qualcomm hardware should see lower overhead and better real-world efficiency, especially in camera-based apps where image buffers are already channel-last.

- 🧩 **Less app-side postprocessing work**\
  By returning semantic class maps directly from exported models, apps no longer need to spend as much CPU time decoding huge segmentation outputs.

- 📈 **Better and more stable semantic segmentation performance**\
  This is especially important for real-time mobile experiences, where unpredictable postprocessing delays can cause lag or jitter.

- 🔒 **More robust export pipeline**\
  Replacing manual ONNX graph surgery with clean wrapper modules makes exports easier to maintain and less error-prone over time.

- 📱🍎 **Benefits extend beyond QNN**
  CoreML semantic exports also gain from the same in-graph class-map idea, so Apple-device deployment gets a speed boost too.

- 🛠️ **Improved reliability for deployment workflows**
  Better RKNN testing, cleaner Docker builds, and more dependable docs publishing all reduce friction for developers working across edge and production environments.

- 👥 **Broad user impact**
  - **Mobile and edge developers** get the biggest benefit from this release.
  - **Semantic segmentation users** should see the clearest speed and usability gains.
  - **General users** also benefit from clearer docs, cleaner CI, and more reliable export behavior.

In short: **v8.4.65 is a strong deployment-focused release** 🎉, with the standout improvement being **faster, more hardware-friendly QNN exports and smarter semantic segmentation outputs for mobile AI**.

### [`v8.4.64`](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/releases/tag/v8.4.64): - Tracker ReID ONNX encoders autodownload (#​24774)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/compare/v8.4.63...v8.4.64)

#### 🌟 Summary

Ultralytics `v8.4.64` makes tracking easier and more reliable 🎯—especially with new auto-downloaded YOLO26 ReID ONNX encoders—while also improving QNN export, multi-GPU training stability, logging, and export robustness 🚀

#### 📊 Key Changes

- **Tracking got a major usability upgrade with auto-downloaded YOLO26 ReID ONNX encoders** 🤖📦\
  You can now use built-in tracking ReID models like `yolo26n-reid.onnx` through `yolo26x-reid.onnx` without manually downloading or exporting them first.

- **Tracking ReID matching is more reliable when appearance features are missing** 🔍\
  TrackTrack now treats missing embeddings as “unknown” instead of assuming they are bad matches, so it can fall back to motion cues more intelligently.

- **QNN export for Qualcomm devices was significantly improved** 📱⚡\
  QNN models now export as a **single self-contained `*_qnn.onnx` file** instead of a folder, with metadata embedded inside. The release also fixes architecture mapping, improves backend loading compatibility, and updates quantization behavior for better Snapdragon deployment.

- **YOLO26x distributed training stability was fixed** 🧠🖥️\
  A DDP deadlock issue affecting some multi-GPU training runs was resolved by restoring handling for unused parameters in conditional branches.

- **MLflow failures no longer crash training** 📉🛡️\
  If MLflow tracking setup or logging fails, training now continues instead of aborting the run.

- **TensorFlow export subprocess calls are safer** 🔐\
  Edge TPU and TensorFlow\.js export commands now avoid shell-based path handling issues, reducing problems with unusual file paths and improving security.

- **Progress/logging output was cleaned up** 🖥️✨\
  Fixed premature `100%` progress display and console log duplication issues, especially useful in platform or remote logging environments.

- **Version checking is more accurate** ✅\
  `parse_version()` now consistently returns 3-part version tuples, fixing incorrect version comparisons like `6.0` vs `6.0.0`.

- **FP16 quantization/export reliability was improved** ⚙️\
  ONNX mixed-precision conversion now uses the correct input name and sample input shape, helping TensorRT/ModelOpt workflows work more consistently.

- **Docs were refreshed across several areas** 📘\
  Updates include clearer tracking/ReID docs, QNN docs, Conda install guidance, hyperparameter tuning explanations, TrackZone behavior, custom trainer checkpoint loading, OpenVINO benchmark references, and terminal visualization guidance.

#### 🎯 Purpose & Impact

- **Easier multi-object tracking setup** 🚀\
  The headline change removes a common setup headache: users can now enable tracking ReID with ready-made YOLO26 ONNX encoders directly, making advanced tracking more accessible to both beginners and production teams.

- **Better tracking quality in difficult scenes** 🎥\
  The ReID fallback improvement should reduce bad associations when objects are briefly occluded or appearance features are unavailable.

- **Simpler Qualcomm deployment** 📱\
  QNN export is now easier to manage and deploy thanks to the single-file output format and improved compatibility across Snapdragon targets.

- **More dependable training at scale** 🖥️\
  Teams training larger YOLO26 models on multiple GPUs should see fewer hangs and more stable runs.

- **Fewer pipeline interruptions** 🛠️\
  MLflow and export-related fixes help ensure optional integrations do not stop core training or deployment workflows.

- **Cleaner user experience** ✨\
  Console logging and progress bar fixes make training output easier to trust and monitor, especially in shared platforms and dashboards.

- **Lower friction for installation and documentation** 📚\
  Updated guides make setup, tuning, export, and custom workflows easier to understand and reproduce.

In short, `v8.4.64` is a **tracking-focused quality-of-life release** with especially strong benefits for users working with **YOLO26 tracking, Qualcomm QNN deployment, and stable training/export pipelines** 🚀

### [`v8.4.63`](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/releases/tag/v8.4.63): - NVIDIA TensorRT 11 support with ModelOpt FP16 and INT8 quantization (#​24735)

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/compare/v8.4.62...v8.4.63)

#### 🌟 Summary

🚀 **Ultralytics v8.4.63 mainly adds TensorRT 11 export support with FP16 and INT8 quantization via NVIDIA ModelOpt, while also expanding built-in multi-object tracking with several new tracker options and improving reliability, performance, and docs.**

#### 📊 Key Changes

- 🧠 **Major export upgrade: TensorRT 11 support**
  - The standout update in this release is PR [#​24735](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/issues/24735) by [@​onuralpszr](https://redirect.github.com/onuralpszr).
  - Ultralytics now supports exporting models to **NVIDIA TensorRT 11**, which had previously broken due to API changes in TensorRT 11.
  - For **FP16** and **INT8** export on TensorRT 11, Ultralytics now uses **NVIDIA ModelOpt** instead of the older TensorRT builder flags and calibrator interface.
  - This keeps export working across:
    - **TensorRT 7–10** with the legacy path
    - **TensorRT 11** with the new strongly-typed ModelOpt path
  - Tested successfully for:
    - `fp32`
    - `fp16`
    - `int8`
    - including **INT8 with dynamic shapes** on TensorRT 11 ✅

- ⚡ **Better quantization workflow for modern NVIDIA deployment**
  - FP16 is now applied by baking mixed precision into the ONNX graph before engine build.
  - INT8 is now applied through explicit quantization in the ONNX graph with calibration data.
  - This is especially important because TensorRT 11 removed the old methods many exporters depended on.

- 🎯 **Big tracking expansion: 4 new built-in trackers**
  - PR [#​24371](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/issues/24371) added four new multi-object trackers alongside BoT-SORT and ByteTrack:
    - **OC-SORT**
    - **Deep OC-SORT**
    - **FastTracker**
    - **TrackTrack**
  - These are now documented and wired into the tracking system with YAML configs like:
    - `ocsort.yaml`
    - `deepocsort.yaml`
    - `fasttrack.yaml`
    - `tracktrack.yaml`

- 🏃 **Tracking docs and selection guidance improved**
  - Tracking docs were expanded to explain the strengths of each tracker and how to choose between them.
  - This makes the tracking feature much easier to use for both beginners and advanced users.

- 📹 **Video stream loading is safer**
  - PR [#​24749](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/issues/24749) improves cleanup when stream initialization fails.
  - If one stream fails while others already opened, Ultralytics now properly closes those partially-opened resources instead of leaking threads or capture handles.

- ⚡ **AI Gym pose workflow is faster**
  - PR [#​24744](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/issues/24744) reduces repeated GPU-to-CPU syncs in the workout monitoring loop by transferring keypoints to CPU in one go instead of piece by piece.
  - Same behavior, better efficiency.

- 🧪 **Validation mixed precision handling simplified**
  - PR [#​24736](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/issues/24736) consolidates validation autocast into one cleaner scope during training validation.
  - This helps keep mixed-precision behavior simpler and more robust.

- 📝 **Documentation improvements**
  - Added new **Rust inference documentation** for running YOLO models through ONNX Runtime without Python.
  - Expanded tracking docs and reference pages.
  - Updated TensorRT and Jetson docs to explain TensorRT 11 behavior and DLA limitations.
  - Refreshed guides like Coral Edge TPU and semantic image search.

#### 🎯 Purpose & Impact

- 🚀 **TensorRT 11 users can export again**
  - This is the biggest user-facing change in the release.
  - If you deploy on modern NVIDIA systems using TensorRT 11, exports that were failing should now work again.
  - This is especially valuable for production inference pipelines and edge/server deployment.

- ⚙️ **Future-proofs NVIDIA deployment**
  - TensorRT 11 changed how precision and quantization are handled.
  - By moving to a ModelOpt-based workflow, Ultralytics stays compatible with newer NVIDIA tooling instead of relying on removed APIs.

- 💾 **Smaller, faster engines remain accessible**
  - FP16 and INT8 exports are still available even with TensorRT 11’s breaking changes.
  - That means users can continue optimizing for:
    - faster inference
    - lower memory use
    - better deployment efficiency

- 📦 **Dynamic INT8 export support is especially useful**
  - Supporting **INT8 with dynamic shapes on TensorRT 11** can help users deploying across varying input sizes without giving up quantization benefits.

- 👀 **Tracking becomes more flexible for real-world scenarios**
  - The new trackers give users more choices depending on their needs:
    - simple baseline tracking
    - crowded-scene tracking
    - appearance-aware tracking
    - occlusion-heavy tracking
  - This can improve results in surveillance, sports, traffic, and retail use cases.

- 🔒 **More stable long-running applications**
  - Stream cleanup improvements reduce the chance of lingering resources in apps that open cameras or network streams.
  - This matters most for production or multi-stream systems.

- ⚡ **Small but meaningful performance wins**
  - AI Gym and validation updates help reduce overhead and improve runtime efficiency without changing how users interact with the API.

Overall, **v8.4.63 is a strong deployment-focused release** 📦—with the headline improvement being **restored and modernized TensorRT 11 export support**, plus a major boost to **tracking capabilities** and several reliability/performance refinements.

#### What's Changed

- Consolidate validation autocast scope by [@​glenn-jocher](https://redirect.github.com/glenn-jocher) in [#​24736](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/pull/24736)
- Convert SAM3 docstrings to Google style by [@​glenn-jocher](https://redirect.github.com/glenn-jocher) in [#​24741](https://redirect.github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics/pull/24741)

reviews.body:
## Summary
Follow-up to PR 2/3. Bringing up the full stack surfaced 8 real failures across Kafka, LocalStack, KMinion, ntfy, Tempo, OTel-collector, Prometheus, and Cruise Control. Each is fixed. Test-plan captured 20/20 containers healthy and 14/14 Prometheus targets UP.

## Fixes

**Compose**
- Pin \`confluentinc/cp-kafka:7.7.1\`, \`cp-schema-registry:7.7.1\`, \`cp-kafka-connect:7.7.1\` (latest CP requires \`advertised.listeners\` on KRaft-only controllers, which is meaningless there).
- Add \`CLUSTER_ID\` env sibling to \`KAFKA_CLUSTER_ID\` on every Kafka container (Confluent init script reads the un-prefixed name).
- Pin \`localstack/localstack:3.8\` (latest = pro/auth-required).
- Pin \`grafana/tempo:2.6.0\` (latest changed the top-level config schema).
- Comment out \`cruise-control\` — no reliable public image; belongs in PR 5 where the metrics-reporter JAR ships with the brokers.
- Disable LocalStack Lambda docker-reuse executor + docker.sock mount: rootless Docker/Podman has no \`/var/run/docker.sock\`. S3/KMS/Secrets still work.
- Drop \`GF_INSTALL_PLUGINS\`: Grafana runs on \`internal: true\` observability network, cannot reach grafana.com.

**Configs**
- \`kminion.yaml\` — rewrite to correct camelCase v2.x schema (\`consumerGroups\`/\`allowedGroups\`/\`topics.allowedTopics\`, \`exporter\` block).
- \`ntfy.yml\` — \`attachment-expiry-duration: \"3h\"\` (empty string rejected as invalid duration).
- \`otel-collector.yaml\` — swap removed \`loki\` exporter for \`otlphttp/loki\` targeting Loki 3.x's OTLP endpoint (\`/otlp\`); drop \`filelog\` receiver (no \`/var/lib/docker/containers\` on rootless).
- \`tempo-config.yaml\` — rewrite to Tempo 2.x monolithic schema; the previous \`metrics_generator\`/\`overrides.defaults\` blocks confused the parser and reported a bogus \"compactor not found\".

**Prometheus**
- Fix \`metrics_path\` indentation on \`loki\`/\`tempo\`/\`pyroscope\` jobs.
- Comment out cruise-control scrape job (matches compose).

## Verified live
- 20/20 containers running
- 14/14 Prometheus scrape targets UP
- Zero JMX/quorum host port leaks (15/15 blocked)
- 10 UIs bound to \`127.0.0.1\`
- Kafka produce → consume round-trip on \`__smoke\` topic
- Blast-radius: edge zone cannot resolve \`controller1\` DNS
- Known gap: obs → broker:9092 open because brokers span obs+data — fixed in the follow-up PR (broker JMX sidecar)

## Depends on
- PR 3 (observability stack) merged to main

- Adds Celery worker scaling tests (`PERF-CEL-001`, `PERF-CEL-002`, `PERF-CEL-003`) and multi-replica Kruize validation (`PERF-ROS-001`) for processing pipeline bottleneck analysis (COST-7598)
- Extracts shared PostgreSQL statistics capture and deployment scaling functions into `k8s_helpers.py`, consolidating logic previously duplicated across `test_db_resource_sweep.py` and the new test file
- Fixes instrumentation bugs: `pg_stat` tuple parsing, active connection count parsing, Kubernetes label selectors for workers/Kruize, and metrics-server lag for freshly scaled pods

### New files
| File | Lines | Purpose |
|------|-------|---------|
| `tests/suites/performance/test_celery_scaling.py` | +884 | Celery replica sweep, OOM threshold, cold/warm characterization, Kruize multi-replica |

### Modified files
| File | Change | Purpose |
|------|--------|---------|
| `k8s_helpers.py` | +174/-0 | PostgreSQL stats (`capture_pg_stats`, `diff_pg_stats`, `get_db_cpu_utilization`, `get_db_shared_buffers`), deployment scaling, tuple parsing fix |
| `test_db_resource_sweep.py` | +3/-142 | Removed duplicated functions, now imports from `k8s_helpers.py` |
| `test_kafka_throughput.py` | +6/-20 | Delegated scaling to shared `k8s_helpers.scale_deployment` |
| `deploy-test-cost-onprem.sh` | +2/-2 | Added `celery` to `--perf-suite` validation allowlist |
| `perf-testing.sh` | +1 | Added `celery` suite mapping |
| `run-pytest.sh` | +7 | Added `--perf-celery` flag |
| `pytest.ini` | +1 | Registered `celery_scaling` marker |

### Test descriptions

**PERF-CEL-001 — Per-queue replica sweep**: Scales OCP, summary, and listener workers through 1/2/3-4 replicas, running 5 concurrent ingestion sources at each level. Captures processing time, DB CPU, worker CPU distribution, and `pg_stat_database` deltas to identify diminishing returns.

**PERF-CEL-002 — Worker OOM threshold**: Constrains OCP worker memory to 256Mi and 512Mi, runs ingestion, and monitors for OOMKill events and pod restarts to determine minimum viable memory limits.

**PERF-CEL-003 — Cold vs warm state characterization**: Runs two sequential ingestion batches on the same deployment, capturing PostgreSQL cache metrics, active connections, and worker pod ages before/after each batch to quantify warm-cache effects.

**PERF-ROS-001 — Multi-replica Kruize validation**: Scales Kruize from 1 to 2 replicas and measures per-pod CPU to validate FINDING-004's single-replica recommendation.

### Bug fixes
- **`pg_stat` parsing**: `execute_db_query` returns pre-split tuples; code was re-splitting `rows[0][0]` on `|`, getting only the first column. Fixed to index the tuple directly
- **Active connections**: `str(rows[0])` on a tuple like `('5',)` produces `"('5',)"`. Fixed to use `rows[0][0]`
- **Worker labels**: Used `app.kubernetes.io/component=celery-worker-ocp` (doesn't exist) and `app.kubernetes.io/name={deploy}` (wrong value). Fixed to `cost-onprem.io/worker-queue=ocp` and `app.kubernetes.io/component=cost-worker`
- **Kruize label**: Used `app.kubernetes.io/component=kruize`. Fixed to `app.kubernetes.io/component=ros-optimization`
- **Pod metrics lag**: `oc adm top pod` doesn't report freshly started pods until metrics-server picks them up (~30-60s). Added `_wait_for_pod_metrics` poll loop (90s timeout) replacing unreliable `sleep(15)`

- [x] Verify no regressions in existing suites

reviews.body:
## Summary

**Launch fullscreen prompt was invisible.** The design-token sweep published `var(--sa-*)` onto *component roots* (HUD, hangar), but the launch prompt attaches elsewhere — so the tokens resolved to nothing there. An unresolved custom property invalidates the **whole declaration**, so the panel lost its background and every line of text fell back to inherited near-black: present and clickable, invisible on screen. Tokens now publish once on `:root` at boot and refresh on content change. One malformed value went with it: `var(--sa-n-800)ee` is not a colour (hex alpha can't be appended to a token), which voided the panel fill even where tokens resolved. Verified with before/after captures; contract tests pin both (tokens resolve on the document element; no stylesheet appends a raw alpha suffix to `var()`).

**Bots stuck nose-to-surface — root cause found on the third attempt.** The previous two fixes reported green metrics because *the harness excluded the failing case*: its stall detector required **powered** contact. A shipped-content harness (`tools/bot-stuck-repro.ts` — real rosters, spawns, colliders, driven through `GameSession` exactly as practice does) reproduced **7 sustained stalls across 100 matches, the worst 578 seconds** nose-first against a Lunar rock.

The mechanism is throttle, not geometry: powered-contact recovery resets below 0.2 throttle, the predictive floor guard requires a descent, and a CTF bot waiting at a blocked base legitimately commands zero throttle. Collision cancels inward velocity but never separates — so a bot at rest against terrain or a rock satisfied *no* recovery condition and stayed for the match.

Recovery is now a **surface-progress invariant** rather than a set of special cases: stationary contact for 1.5s triggers it regardless of throttle, attitude, descent or utility plan; it reorients along the measured outward normal, holds thrust while still pointing inward, then drives to 4 units of real clearance before resuming the objective.

| Metric (20 seeds × 600s, doubled Lunar) | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Sustained-stuck bots | 7 | **0** |
| Worst stationary contact | 578.43 s | **4.17 s** |
| Windows > 5 s | 7 | **0** |

The regression parks a zero-throttle hull nose-down on the shipped collision plane and nose-first against a shipped rock; it **fails with the new watchdog disabled**.

reviews.body:
Supporting regression put two very different kinds of number into the same table, and the frontend formatted them identically. A bounded score sits in [0, 1]; an error term is in the units of the target and might be 54.75 or 128,456.79. One `toFixed(4)` cannot serve both:

  0.9561       -> 0.9561        fine
  128456.7891  -> 128456.7891   four decimals on six digits
  0.00003      -> 0.0000        every digit lost, silently

That last case is the one that matters: a small metric rendered as zero with nothing to indicate it had been rounded away. Regression predictions had the mirror problem — String(152.13381958007812) prints seventeen digits, the model's binary precision presented as confidence.

lib/format.ts now decides presentation from the magnitude of the value, never from the metric's name. Name matching would tie the UI to one project's vocabulary, and a pipeline logging test_mape has to display with no frontend change — the same rule that keeps the prediction form dataset-agnostic, applied to numbers.

Extract the markup the three pages had been repeating: the page-header block appeared in all three, the table wrapper in three places, and seven section headings each re-stated their own empty state. Pages now compose PageHeader, Section, DataTable, KeyValueTable, MetricGrid, and ProbabilityBars. DataTable takes its columns as data rather than markup, which is what already let the runs dashboard derive columns from whatever metrics MLflow reported.

Two consistency fixes fell out of that rather than needing their own pass. Empty states were mixed — some sections rendered the standard card, others a bare paragraph — and now all route through Section. Timestamps are relative with the absolute in a title, since "3 hours ago" answers "is this the run I just started?" faster than a full date.

Also: probability bars gained meter roles and labels; numeric table cells use tabular figures so digits align down a column; .vite was added to .prettierignore, without which `npm run lint` fails after any dev-server run because the cache is checked for formatting; and five unlabelled code fences in architecture.md are now marked as text.

Verified against a live stack holding both a regression and a classification run: bounded scores render at four decimals (accuracy=0.9561, r2=0.4395) and error terms at two (rmse=54.50, mae=43.94), from the same table with no per-metric configuration.

Frontend tests: 18 -> 38. Backend unchanged at 100.
